examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
examples.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.$
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
If we let $u=6{x}^{2},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=12x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=12x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\sqrt{\pi /12}$ | $\sqrt{\pi /6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /2$ | $\pi $ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /12}}^{\sqrt{\pi /6}}12x\operatorname{cos}⁡(6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /12}}^{\sqrt{\pi /6}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6{x}^{2})\cdot 12x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u)\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0-1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$
